item.content:encoded: Most online attacks don’t happen in one step.A phishing link leads to a fake site, the site pushes a malicious download, and the download delivers the payload.As someone who works online every day, I already think about security in layers, so having phishing, scam, and malware protection alongside the VPN is useful to me.NordVPN’s built-in next-gen antivirus aims to intercept threats earlier in the attack pipeline instead of waiting until a malicious file has already reached your device. NordVPN uses a proprietary machine learning model to block phishing sites before they cause harm, while its malware protection scans downloading files and removes them if they’re dangerous.Anti-phishing protection powered by NordVPN’s proprietary machine-learning modelProtection against scam websites and fake online storesMalware scanning for downloading filesThe VPN remains a core part of NordVPN, alongside these additional security features.Depending on your plan and operating system, one subscription gives you access to multiple security tools.Plus, it comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee.(Thanks to NordVPN for partnering on this newsletter.) was supposed to make the web faster.It introduced multiplexing, header compression & better connection reuse.But one lost TCP packet could still delay every stream on the connection. was built to solve this problem.In this newsletter, we’ll break down 12 essential concepts behind & :HPACK header compression,Server push & early hints,TCP head-of-line blocking,Independent streams & loss recovery,Connection IDs & connection migration,Alt-Svc & HTTPS DNS records.What it is & how it works in simple words,Multiplexing sends many requests & responses at the same time over ONE connection by interleaving their frames.Request one waits on a slow database while other requests return & render. The server replies in whatever order the data becomes ready.The result shows up plainly in connection counts:A desktop page opens connections on than on . The gap roughly doubles on lighter pages, where one connection does the work of two.One conversation channel where each sentence carries the speaker’s name.Three people talk at once, and nobody loses the thread.Multiplexing changes how you bundle because many tiny files beat a large one for cache reuse.Confirm which protocol your assets use with the devtools protocol column and measure the bundling change in WebPageTest. Yet TCP head-of-line blocking marks the limit multiplexing could never remove.13. HPACK Header CompressionHPACK is the header compression format for .It’s built from a static table, a dynamic table & Huffman coding.Headers repeat almost perfectly. Your string, headers, and go out identically on every request, and on an API-heavy page they outweigh the payload.A fixed table of common header names covers the obvious cases, so a method line becomes a single byte. Headers you have already sent go into a dynamic table shared by both ends.The second request references those entries by number rather than repeating them, and the saving compounds across every request on the connection.Shorthand between two colleagues who talk daily.Once you both agree a short name means one specific document, you stop saying the full title.Header weight decides real latency on pages carrying large authentication tokens.Inspect encoded header sizes in Wireshark and compare them against the devtools network panel. QPACK rebuilds this idea for out-of-order delivery.Flow control limits how much data a sender may have outstanding, applied per stream & across the whole connection.The receiver sets a flow-control window. This limits how much DATA the sender can transmit before receiving additional flow-control credit. A frame grants more room as the receiver consumes data, and the default initial window is 65,535 bytes.This mechanism protects slow consumers:A browser decoding a large image should slow the pipe rather than buffer forever, and a proxy feeding a slow client behaves the same way.Also it stops one greedy stream from monopolizing a connection everything else depends on.A coworker saying, “Send me five files at a time, and I will ask for more.”They control the pace, so nothing piles up on their desk.Large uploads, gRPC streams, and video segments all hit this ceiling before they hit bandwidth.Watch window updates with and confirm socket-level throughput with . Independent streams show how QUIC applies the same idea per stream.15. Stream PrioritizationStream prioritization lets a client tell the server which responses matter most, so the server can send that data first.A browser needs CSS to render a webpage. Giving CSS higher priority than a large image helps the page become usable quicker, even if the total amount of data stays the same. used a complex system of stream dependencies & weights to decide which data to send first. But browsers & servers struggled to implement it consistently!Then a simpler priority scheme got introduced... It uses 2 signals: Indicates how important a response is. Zero is the highest priority & seven is the lowest. Indicates whether a response can be delivered progressively, thus allowing the server to interleave its data with other responses.Also browsers provide the Fetch Priority API.This lets developers influence the priority of resources using attributes such as .The browser uses these hints when scheduling requests and assigning HTTP priorities, although the Fetch Priority API does not directly expose HTTP’s urgency values.Adoption of the Fetch Priority API grew rapidly after Chrome introduced support.Everyone in the waiting room gets seen & order reflects who needs help soonest.One attribute on your largest visible image moves a headline performance metric.Set fetchpriority in your markup and verify the assigned value in the Chrome devtools priority column. Early hints reach the same goal from the server side.16. Server Push and Early HintsServer Push lets a server send resources to a browser before browser requests them.It was one of ’s most promising features.Servers pushed files already stored in the browser’s cache, thus wasting bandwidth. Also performance improvements were inconsistent, so adoption remained low.(Chrome eventually disabled Server Push by default, and Firefox removed support.)Early Hints emerged as a simpler alternative:Instead of sending the resource itself, the server sends an HTTP response containing headers while preparing the final response.The browser then uses these hints to: Establish connections to other servers before they’re needed. Start downloading crucial resources, such as CSS files, before the final HTML arrives.This helps the browser start useful work earlier & potentially render the page faster.Yet adoption remains limited… Only 2.9% of desktop pages used Early Hints, with Shopify accounting for roughly 90% of those deployments.Push is a waiter setting down a dish you never ordered & may already have.Early hints is a waiter handing you the menu while the kitchen warms up.Dead push configuration survives in production long after browsers stopped honoring it.Enable early hints at Cloudflare/Fastly and prove the gain with real user monitoring rather than a lab score. Chunked transfer encoding fills the same dead time once the response finally starts.17. TCP Head-of-Line BlockingTCP delivers data to applications in a strict order.If a TCP packet gets lost, later data must wait until the missing packet gets retransmitted. Yet this creates a problem for … multiplexes multiple streams over one TCP connection. And TCP sees only a single ordered sequence of bytes, with no knowledge of individual streams. So one lost TCP packet delays data delivery across multiple streams, even when their data has already arrived.This is called TCP head-of-line () blocking.TCP uses acknowledgments & retransmissions to provide reliable, ordered delivery.But this ordering can delay otherwise available data… On lossy networks, using one TCP connection sometimes performs worse than using six parallel connections.Each TCP connection handles packet loss independently, so a lost packet on one connection does not directly block the others.One conveyor belt at a sorting depot.Drop a box & everything behind it stops moving, even if those parcels have nothing to do with each other.This single property is the entire reason exists.Confirm retransmits with and capture the stall itself with . QUIC over UDP replaces the transport rather than working around it.When you upgrade, you’ll get:High-level architecture of real-world systems.Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.(If this newsletter has helped you become a better software engineer, consider subscribing to support my work.)

It is a large hybrid reasoning model (671B parameters, 37B active) that supports both thinking and non-thinking modes. It extends the DeepSeek-V3 base with a two-phase long-context training process, reaching up to 128K tokens, and uses FP8 microscaling for efficient inference. Users can control the reasoning behaviour with the boolean. The model improves tool use, code generation, and reasoning efficiency, achieving performance comparable to DeepSeek-R1 on difficult benchmarks while responding more quickly. It supports structured tool calling, code agents, and search agents, making it suitable for research, coding, and agentic workflows.

item.title: Steam For Linux Finally Goes 64-Bit
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Valve has released a new Steam Client beta that finally moves the Linux client to 64-bit architecture, while also placing it inside a containerized Steam Runtime environment. However, Linux users still need 32-bit libraries and graphics drivers for compatibility, meaning fully 64-bit-only systems remain unsupported. VideoCardz.com reports: Valve's updated requirements explicitly state that 64-bit-only installations are not supported. Systems must still provide both 32-bit and 64-bit libraries and graphics drivers, including multilib support. The new client also requires Linux kernel 5.6 or newer and glibc 2.31 or newer.
The update also introduces Steam Achievement Sets, a feature we covered earlier that allows developers to organize achievements into separate groups for base games, DLCs and seasonal content. Players can complete individual sets without losing their existing completion status when developers add more achievements. Valve has also updated the achievements page to display progress across these groups.
The 64-bit Linux client and Achievement Sets are currently available through the Steam Client Beta. Valve has not confirmed when these changes will reach the stable Linux release. Until then, users on the regular Steam client will continue using the existing architecture.

item.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
item.author: gmays
item.content:encoded: Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.Try it in the BFL API · Download the weightsLeading open weights quality with fewer parametersIn internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.On the speed–quality frontierFLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.If you use FLUX 3 Image Klein in your work, please cite:@misc{bfl2026flux3imageklein, author = {{Black Forest Labs}}, title = {{FLUX} 3 Image Klein}, year = {2026}, url = {https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein}, }

item.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
item.author: pretext
item.content:encoded: We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEWClaude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.Code review does two jobs:Find and fix issues before they shipBuild shared context and codebase understanding across the teamThis article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"Asking that question also changed review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTIONWe want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.A typical Claude Code change, from the author's machine to usersSix layers of checks, with rollback under them1. The work is verified before anyone else looksMost review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as: tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date., written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.2. AI review on every pull requestEvery pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and runs a lighter version locally.When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.3. Security review that can blockSecurity gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.4. Automated checks that blockThe usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.5. Human approval, scaled by riskA docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are greenOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleThe change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual releaseThe merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the channel first. The channel trails it.7. Fast detection, fast rollbackSome mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTEROur code review process is constantly improving in a loop.Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.Our incidents are the evalBuilt from past incidents and reverts, run every dayWe measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review: After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach. after the first few passes. so the author fixes every instance, not one line. of findings already posted.Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else.Internal pull requests, before and after the convergence changesWHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOPPulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at:Should we build this at all? Direction, taste and scope. One team that declared its review bottleneck solved still kept human review for changes from outside the team, so someone asks "should we even do this?" such as billing, the auto-updater and CI workflows. that sets a pattern others will copy. Test output, the command that ran and what it returned, a screenshot, the reviewer's findings. If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval. A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it.Five decisions stay with people; checks run everywhere elseSHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAMCode review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn.If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it."YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly: so they're easy to review, debug and revert.Everything is reversible. Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes.Blast radius sets the bar. Expensive code gets more people and more checks. through telemetry and internal use. Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system.Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR.Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR.HOW YOU CAN ADOPT THIS PROCESSMost of the pieces to do this with your team exist today.Give your agent checks it can run, listed in a short , plus hooks that run formatters and linters.Run and locally, or a fresh-context subagent review.Add a , and move repeated review comments into it.Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune for a few weeks, then widen.Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a , a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.

item.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
item.author: ahlCVA
item.content:encoded: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue., Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp () for some number of iterations (). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed.This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator , which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.Claude found some base points tooBut wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.The recipe here is simple:Seed the generator with a small integer.Throw away seven outputs.Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.Code to reproduce the seedsCode to reproduce selected base pointsTo the extent possible under law, the authors have waived all copyright and related or neighboring rights to the code on this page, dedicating it to the public domain under CC0 1.0 Universal ().

Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
item.author: pretext
item.content:encoded: Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv.Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as —which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer. Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classicalalgorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum . These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2). In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components. Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.A new reversible algorithmDesigning a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs. The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.A hard first test: modular inversionThe first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself times, find . For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.The memory demands of divstepsMost of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer , find such that ≡ 1 (mod ). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called . Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called , is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.How Claude got around the memory problemClaude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history. Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).Optimizing a quantum optimizerOptimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.A more efficient quantum decoderThe researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position contains several acceptable values of . The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed-Solomon decoder.Reed-Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a . The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed-Solomon decoding.So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp-Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp-Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.A simplified approach to storageSwitching to Berlekamp-Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information. Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones. We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost. This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.We thank Arjun Kar and Vinay Ramasesh for helpful discussions in the early stages of the project.

item.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in theBenchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

item.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
item.author: farlight
item.content:encoded: JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot.jixel, a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl, except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data.AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.AVIF is faster to decode.
