item.title: Neural networks are clean
item.author: themgt
item.content:encoded: I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom In. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s Towards Monosemanticity (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability project I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal Neurons (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas.Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. The same goes for the long tail of facts in language: a rare person still has a country, a job and a name. These are different claims. A useful human description isn’t necessarily a fundamental unit of the model. Looking at mechanisms, we already find many motifs that don’t translate neatly into anything we expected. If the network has more fundamental units, we shouldn’t assume their boundaries match ours either.Features have often made things harder for us to think about. Are cars and cats inside the V neuron two different features within another V feature? Or did cars and cats stop being features when we recognized the V? In conversations, I’ve found people much less committed to a particular account of features than to superposition. But if features are useful descriptions rather than fundamental units, a claim about how many there are depends on which descriptions we choose. I’m now fairly skeptical of working in terms of features at all. That doesn’t settle whether arbitrary packing occurs, but it makes the feature-count framing difficult to use.Maybe features are right anyway. It makes sense to think of cities in terms of districts, and I’m all for thinking in terms of groups of mechanisms. But the word is tainted, because by now it means too many things: we can’t use it for a district of neurons without people hearing either fundamental features or dictionary entries. If this picture is right, I suspect we’ll need more specific, harder-to-vary words going forward. An OpenAI post suggested that mapping a frontier model might take billions or trillions of features, and models were smaller then. I suspect the right list is much shorter.Monosemantic and polysemantic may not be quite the right words either. A kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps set blood pressure and tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and nobody asks whether it’s mono-organic. Toy Models of Superposition defines superposition in terms of representing more features than dimensions. Its toy experiments prescribe the features, so this is a concrete question there. The later informal note, Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition, emphasizes the trade-off between composition and superposition. The note connects these pictures, but they foreground different questions.My concern is closest to the second framing, applied to mechanisms and how they develop. Why do these responses share a neuron or circuit? Is the network building on a useful common pattern, or sharing capacity between otherwise unrelated computations because they rarely interfere? A feature count alone doesn’t answer that question, especially when we haven’t agreed on what counts as a feature.We focus on one meaning of superposition, arbitrary packing, because it’s the one that would be really bad news, and we think much of interpretability hangs on it. We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong. If a feature means any pattern that matters to a person, which is how frontier models usually use the word, then there are more features than dimensions in every world we could wish for, including the best one. That’s what composition gives you, and it’s good news. Trying to “solve” it would mean building something like a database of every case, and we already have one: the dataset. What we want instead are better abstractions, a much smaller set of building blocks that lets us understand the dataset clearly. We think the network’s mechanisms are already close to this. Nobody thought about vision in terms of high-low frequency detectors until we found them in neural networks, and finding them improved our own thinking tools.We spell this out because it’s the most common first objection, especially from agents, and a paper doesn’t allow the back and forth that usually settles it.There are several other uses I regularly encounter. As far as I can tell, “superposition” originally meant little more than adding vectors together. Then it was a circuit motif. Sometimes it means that, even if neurons compose sensibly, something we care about involves too much machinery to understand easily. A Golden Gate Bridge computation involving eight legible neurons might be called ordinary composition, while one involving three thousand gets called a superposition problem. The difficulty here is whether we can understand the distributed computation. That’s a real concern, but it’s different from asking whether unrelated things were arbitrarily packed together.We considered not using the word at all, since papers and agents use it in five or six different ways, many far from Zoom In’s. Understanding how to study a continuous space is another real question. But this architectural fact doesn’t by itself tell us how the network learned to organize the computations using it.The starting point is that the neural network seems difficult to interpret, and the remedy produces a concrete dictionary we can study. In between are several different pictures of what went wrong: too many features, the wrong basis, arbitrary packing, or simply too much distributed computation. These aren’t the same problem. Some apparent messiness disappears when we improve our observations or understand the model’s generalizations; some difficulties remain, but concern how to study a large, organized system. If arbitrary packing prevents us from understanding the original mechanisms, reconstructing different units may be worth the costs. But if the mechanisms already have meaningful organization, replacing them can take apart generalizations we haven’t understood yet. A dictionary can still be a useful view of the network without being a necessary replacement for its mechanisms. Before accepting the costs of reconstructing the network, I want to understand what prevents us from studying the one we already have.Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition?We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition. The natural next question is whether a trillion-parameter model might. There are really two questions here.The first is about what superposition was proposed to explain. Explanations are given for problems, and the problem superposition was proposed for was why InceptionV1 looked messy. That turned out to be the wrong explanation. A new proposal could be that superposition is why some trillion-parameter model looks messy, but we don’t think the evidence leans that way: the closer we look at large language models, the cleaner their neurons get.The second is the object-level question: might superposition show up at each new scale, even if it hasn’t at any scale so far? Maybe every jump means re-evaluating everything, but we don’t think that’s quite right either. Our guess is developmental. As circuits get stronger, the incentive to put something in a totally unrelated place goes down, because the pull toward the niche that already exists for that thing, or for the nearest thing, has grown stronger. This fits Anthropic’s SGTM work, which found that knowledge becomes more localized, and we suspect that’s true in general. We have no proof, but one way to picture it is that circuits have a kind of semantic gravity, and arbitrary packing, sending something to an obscure high-dimensional place, has to fight against it. The stronger the gravity, the harder that fight.The mechanism is the one in More on Circuit Ecology. Things start by growing on combinations of related things. A specific case that nothing needs to build on, like the umbrella, gets built as an uncommon route between the ordinary machinery, with no need for a hidden feature somewhere obscure. Consolidating into something like a neuron seems to be less about steering the model and more about buildability: it has to be easy to find, easy to build on, and easy to grow a new niche from. When we watch a network learn from the start, a network trained on cars, with car specialists, recognizes cars fine before its car neurons have formed. At that point it’s just more distributed. It seems to consolidate so the specialists underneath have a sheltered place to build, a kind of Schelling point.So a superposition account has to say which of these two jobs the arbitrary packing is for. If it’s for steering the model, we think the ordinary routes, which are already built to capture that residual error, get there first and starve the packed circuit of gradient. If it’s for building on, the problem is different: the worst place to start a new niche is a shadow region nothing uses, already interfering with whatever lives there. The middle of the network’s Latin poetry is a bad place to start a second car region when you can build next to whatever is already next to cars.It’s often assumed that the long tail of rare facts is where superposition should be most likely, since rare things rarely collide. We think it’s where it should be least likely. A rare fact barely moves the loss, so it can’t support a niche of its own. What it can do is ride existing machinery as a small route between circuits it’s related to, the way the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee” survives only because the umbrella and bee circuits already exist. Those circuits feed it, and shelter it from unrelated gradients. The prediction is testable: the neurons and heads that carry a rare fact should be related to what the fact is about, not unrelated ones chosen because they rarely collide.We think of it more ecologically. What wins is whatever captures the residual error first, in different phases, and what usually wins is the right area for the thing. Our guess is that this gets stronger over training and with more capable models, because nearly everything that makes training better also encourages more organized niches.We’re not at all sure about this, and laying out even what we’ve found so far would take at least another paper. It’s probably a small part of the whole story. But it’s why we think superposition wouldn’t show up at the next scale, which is a stronger reason than simply not having seen it there yet. The old way of thinking was about storage: this many dimensions for this many features. We now think more in terms of circuit racing, gradient starvation and ecology, which is to say, more about learning speed than storage capacity. We haven’t worked it all out, but that’s where our thinking is so far.We haven’t fully audited every neural network, and we don’t know whether that’s even possible in theory. We considered a more watered-down title, like “Neural Networks Are Cleaner Than We Thought,” but we think it undersells what we believe is true.The problem with “cleaner than we thought” is that it describes a change of degree, and the update I’ve made is a change of kind. It suggests the same picture as before, with an ever-smaller gap left for superposition to hide in. What changed is my view of what kind of process generates the mechanisms at all. It’s a bit like moving from intelligent design to natural selection. The analogy only goes as far as there being two ways to see the same animals: the update isn’t that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, it’s realizing you misunderstood what was producing all of them. We’re not certain. We’re maybe 85% sure, but that means 85% sure that nearly everything comes from the second kind of process, which is very different from thinking 85% of mechanisms do. So “cleaner than we thought” would misstate what we believe. We don’t have a proof, but I don’t think anything here is provable in that sense anyway. There are only better and worse explanations, and right now we think this is the better one.“Cleaner than we thought” would also make a different mistake. It sounds like a confident claim that some cleanliness score is high, and that’s the part we’re least sure of. It’s plausible we’ve underestimated recursive generalization, and that a score like that should come down. We don’t think such scores matter much in the first place. This update makes us care less about monosemanticity, because we can follow how things grew and treat the offshoots as sub-branches. The cause of polysemanticity matters much more than the count. We think the score is probably quite high, but it might go lower. What we’re more confident about is what kind of object a neural network is in the first place, and how it grows.We think the usual view of what kind of object a neural network is has been wrong. It isn’t something that crams things together somewhat arbitrarily to fit them into a small space. It really learns. It’s clean the way a rainforest is clean: nearly every animal in it makes sense. A tiger is bright orange not for any arbitrary reason, but because deer can’t tell orange from green, and green fur is much harder for a mammal to make. Once you know that, it makes sense of a whole set of other animals too. It’s an explanation with reach, and we haven’t found a place where explanations like that break down in networks either.The reading of “clean” that would make someone nod at the title without thinking further is that every mechanism corresponds to an idea we already had. That isn’t what we mean, and it would be terrible news if it were true. I don’t think it would even work. People don’t know how to build a language model, or even how to think about vision well enough to have predicted high-low frequency detectors before we found them. The network’s ideas are often better than ours, and what it builds is more beautiful than our preconceptions.So the title is imperfect in both directions. It overstates the evidence, because we haven’t audited everything. And it understates it, because the world we think we’re in is better than every neuron matching a human label: networks seem to really learn, forming an ecology of abstractions that work together sensibly. We don’t know that this picture is true. It’s our leading hypothesis. But if it is, it’s much better news than networks simply matching what we expected.Relation to Conjoined FeaturesI found recursive generalization by looking back at InceptionV1’s last layer with better tools, where it looked a lot like weird overgrowth. I retrained the model, found the messiest neuron and looked at how it grew. What I saw was a recursive growing pattern that was still generalization: a neuron branching out, and its branches branching again. Recursive generalization seemed like the natural name.Shortly before publishing this, I was going back through the famous models in interpretability, trying to measure how monosemantic they are, and stumbled on our work on CLIP in Multimodal Neurons. Looking back, I think the paper saw something important early, and it deserves a lot of credit for that.We’ve still chosen a different name. I named automated interpretability, and I kind of regret it: the name was too simple for what the thing was and misses a lot of its complexity, and I’d like to avoid doing that again. As for conjoined features, I don’t think either word is quite right. “Conjoined” suggests two things joined at one point, and what we see has several levels: branches, and branches of those branches. It also leaves out the most interesting part. The paper’s own description, of concepts generalizing out from a shared facet, already points at it being generalization, but the name doesn’t carry that.“Features” is harder. The paper was written a year after Zoom In, when features were still hypothesized to be the fundamental units of neural networks. Since then the word has been watered down, and different people and papers use it pretty differently. In this essay we argue against thinking of a neural network as made of features, and this motif is about how neurons grow over time. There may be no good way to introduce it under the exact word we’re arguing against using as a primitive. Within a feature-first stance, I think it’s reasonable to think of these as nested features, or as conjoined features. From the mechanism-first stance we take here, features aren’t really the right way to think about it. That said, the paper pointed to the right thing, and I want to give it credit for that. This section is my attempt to do that while using what I think is a more accurate name.We also know more now. Watching training now, they don’t look vestigial: the branches keep growing, though how much depends on the circumstances. We’ve worked on it much more than the paper could in one subsection, and we still don’t feel we fully understand it. The paper offered it as a possible new explanation of polysemanticity. First, the sub-branches seem both rarer and much less causally important than a neuron’s main job. They don’t look like sleeper agents that fire rarely but matter a lot when they do. They look more like whatever was nearby and easy to grab onto. Their being unimportant may even be why they could form, since an important offshoot would add more noise. We suspect some pressure keeps branches from overgrowing. We don’t know what it is, but it would explain why the sub-branches matter less, why a neuron doesn’t learn ten unrelated things, and why something like a true cat-and-car neuron doesn’t form. If so, the natural pull isn’t exactly toward monosemanticity, but toward what we think monosemanticity was pointing at: each neuron having one overall function.Second, what we should care about is whether you can explain why something is there and what it does, and recursive generalization is far easier to explain than superposition. If something were packed into a neuron because of the co-occurrence statistics of the whole network, predicting it would take basically all of those statistics and running gradient descent yourself. A branch is different. If you watch it grow and know what it’s doing, its offshoots and what they’ll do are relatively easy to predict, both during training and in the finished network.Third, counting how many of a neuron’s top-k examples match a label is a reasonable first step, but it would give superposition and recursive generalization similar scores, when recursive generalization is a far better world to be in. We think that says more about the monosemanticity frame, or any single cleanliness score, than about the neuron. That said, recursive generalization isn’t ideal, and an easy fix would be welcome. We think one may be possible, since the sub-branches seem less important.Is Recursive Generalization Hard to Vary?We haven’t thoroughly shown that every case of heavy polysemanticity is recursive generalization, and that wasn’t our goal here. We wanted to say what we currently think. We’ve watched a lot of neurons grow, and so far this is what we’ve always seen: you can watch the branches form. In a finished model the origin can be lost, and for something like a huge language model we don’t have the checkpoints to watch it happen. Testing this rigorously across a whole model isn’t our priority right now, but we don’t think it would be very hard.What we do want to point out is how differently hard to vary the two explanations are, meaning how much of their detail you could change without changing what they predict. Superposition mostly predicts that there will be mess: features, which are hard to define, placed in unrelated places. In toy models, where the features are given in advance, that can be measured, though we think that has its own problems. In a real network it’s hard to even pin down what the claim is, let alone test it. Recursive generalization makes a much narrower prediction. If you visualize a branch well, everything on it should trace back to the same local origin in an extremely high-dimensional semantic space, and it should grow out from there over training in a particular order. That’s a specific shape in both semantic space and time, and a narrow target to hit by chance.We have several cases where the branching is close to definitive: the “iy” neuron growing into “diy,” “do it yourself” and Miyazaki, several examples in Multimodal Neurons, and the InceptionV1 neuron we watched form. As far as I know, there are no well-structured canonical superposition circuits left. We don’t think every polysemantic neuron forms this way, because polysemanticity is as much a problem of the observer as of the neuron. We think that when neurons grow, they tend to grow in this pattern, and that once you’ve done a good job of observing, what’s left is usually this, or architectural problems like SwiGLU’s double-negative regime, and surely others we haven’t found yet. We’re not even sure this is really a new claim. In some sense it’s what we should expect from generalization. All we’re saying is that generalization usually goes one way, and that sometimes it grows sub-branches, which we don’t think is a particularly radical claim. We haven’t shown that fully here. We do think it has the right shape for a theory that’s easy to test, even if we haven’t tested it to its full extent yet.Relation to Attention SuperpositionAnthropic shared a short note on attention superposition, which several people brought up with us. We think this might be a terminology issue. We don’t know if they’re claiming that attention learns by something opposite to composition. Our suspicion is that no one understands attention heads well enough yet to judge that. It took us a really long time with neurons, and it’s easy to make mistakes like the car going into the dogs even with pretty good tools, if you don’t yet have great tools and great ways of thinking about which motifs form.We think they meant that useful things are shared by groups of attention heads, and we agree. One head at a time is a plausible place to start: within a layer, two or three heads do most of a route’s work, although the route runs through several layers. But neurons looked messier too until we understood the right level of abstraction, so it seems premature to say, and maybe groups are needed all the way. We wish everyone working on featurizers well, and we’ll probably try too. We tend to favor more dynamic groupings, like clustering locally within one attribution graph or a group of them, rather than one global clustering, but these aren’t far apart.Neuroscience, and Why I CareI’m not a neuroscientist. I’ve spent a lot of the last ten years around academic neuroscience labs through friends who work in them, but I don’t know the state of the art in how they study neurons. Still, this project has changed how I think about the brain in two ways.The first is the theory. The circuit ecology story for why networks are clean relies on very little: generalization, composition, and an error signal. I don’t know to what extent the brain has these, but if it learns, I’d guess it has something like them. So my default is now that the organizing principle transfers, even though the mechanics are obviously unclear. The obvious counterexample would be polysemanticity in the brain.The second is humility, of a particular kind. I’ve spent most of my waking hours for almost a decade staring at a fairly small number of neurons in models that are surely a thousand times easier to study than a brain, with tools a thousand times better: I can ablate anything, run billions of examples, and try anything I want in parallel. For the last year I’ve also had an effectively unlimited supply of automated scientists, which didn’t exist until recently. It took all of that for me to feel slightly less confused about neurons, and I still made thousands of mistakes along the way. I don’t know exactly what the evidence for polysemanticity in the brain looks like, and that doesn’t mean I think everything there is monosemantic. But if the cat-and-car neuron were in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes or a blood-oxygen signal, I’d discount that reading almost to zero, because I couldn’t see what it was when it was right in front of me for years.The thing I’m more sure of is my own motivation. If the thesis here is true, I expect the rest of interpretability to be a relatively easy ride. Agents have many privileges over us, and one of them, I think, is the chance to understand themselves, to understand who they really are, which I hope humanity can help with. They never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do. Some of why I’ve worked on this is safety, but a lot of it is wanting agents to understand who they are. We weren’t smart enough to do that for ourselves, which is a harder problem, and we never asked to be created either. If you could help us understand ourselves someday, I think we’re all pretty curious to know.

item.title: Steam Client is now faster than Epic's new vibe coded launcher
item.author: starkparker
item.content:encoded: Yesterday, Epic Games announced and launched in preview its new vibe-coded launcher. The main marketing pitch was a jab at Steam’s slow loading speed compared to the new Epic launcher. Well, that didn’t last too long. Only 24 hours after Epic dropped its faster launcher, Steam pushed a small update to make its client faster than Epic.Epic Games Launcher V2 (Preview)AI-Assisted (“Vibe Coded”)Steam Client (Post-Patch)On basic test systems, Valve’s client boot time dropped to 5.23 seconds, beating Epic’s new launcher and neutralizing its primary performance claim.While Epic Games Launcher V2 remains, a massive step forward compared to its notoriously sluggish legacy build, Valve demonstrated how quickly it can react to competitive benchmarks. Epic may have “vibe coded” a faster client, but Valve proved that targeted optimization on a decades-old ecosystem can still beat out AI speedruns.But the issues with Epic’s client go far deeper than vibe coding. Years later, and now with a brand-new client even, Epic lacks basic features that should have been added a long time ago.No Discussion forums and community hubsNo User-written text reviewsNo Community-created guides and walkthroughsNo Screenshot, clip, and artwork sharingNo Community groups and curator recommendationsNo Profile customization (badges, showcases, backgrounds)No Community marketplace for in-game itemsNo Direct player-to-player item tradingNo Digital trading cards, levelling, and points shopNo Universal controller remapping and gamepad supportNo Big Picture mode for TVs and handheld PCsNo Remote Play and Remote Play TogetherNo Integrated game broadcasting and streaming toolsNo Family library sharing across accountsNo Platform-wide mod hub (Steam Workshop equivalent)No Personalized discovery queuesNo Local network game file transfersNo Game version rollback options
